content.thinking:
The samples directory seems empty, so I'll move on. I'm planning the structure as plain objects needing a builder with exactly one root joint—I'll set up a "root" joint at the origin, then add joints for moving parts like a hinged chest lid and possibly spike trap spikes.

I'm sketching the overall layout: a stone floor slab roughly 2.8 x 2.0 meters sitting flush at y=0, with a back stone brick wall behind it holding two wall torches flanking a chest, keeping the composition simple but visually grounded.

For the chest, I'm placing it slightly left of center with its lid hinged open to reveal a pile of gold coins inside. On the right side I'm arranging three barrels—two upright and one tipped on its side with a loose lid—using a faceted lathe shape to keep the pixel-art blocky look, then planning to paint vertical wood-plank stripes onto them with cell-shaded coloring.

Working through barrel stave texturing...

I want to compute the angle from each cell's position relative to a barrel's center to determine stave index, with a seam midway through each face, wrapped in a reusable paint function taking center coordinates and seed. Next I'm planning a bone pile prop on the left front, starting with a pixel-art skull built from boxes with textured eye sockets.

Then I'm sketching the ribcage as curved sweep geometry using box cross-sections for a blocky look, plus femurs, scattered vertebrae, and a hand bone. For the spike trap, I'm laying out a recessed stone floor plate with a 4x4 grid of pyramid-shaped iron spikes of varying retracted heights, blood stains, and a rusty pressure plate, possibly with a bone caught on one spike. Finally I'm planning two wall torches with iron brackets, wrapped cloth heads, and crossed-card flame textures for the glow effect.

I'm adding a floor brazier with a bowl flame plus a dropped, burnt-out torch lying near the bones for storytelling detail, along with dungeon clutter like cobwebs, moss patches, cracked floor paint, puddles, rubble, spilled coins, and a wall-mounted chain shackle for atmosphere. I'm settling on a texel scale of roughly 0.02m for large surfaces and 0.01–0.0125m for small details, with a 1024-texel paint sheet for the cell-shaded textures.

Now I'm working out texture resolution — estimating total painted surface area (floor plus walls, around 15 m²) to figure out the right texel density, which pushes me toward a 2048 or even 4096 atlas for crispness, or alternatively building the stone wall and floor from tiled brick boxes with procedural pixel textures sized to match the face dimensions.

Planning brick courses with alternating widths, bayer-dithered shading, mortar lines, moss patches, cracks, and torch soot stains drawn directly into the wall tile at known torch pixel coordinates, plus chain mounting details.

Now I'm working out the coordinate mapping for the front face texture, converting pixel positions to world space, and carefully reasoning through orientation since viewer-left versus model-left get confusing when the model faces +Z and the camera looks toward -Z.

I'm also considering adding architectural details to the wall, like a stone baseboard ledge or protruding brick accents, to make the surface feel less flat.

I'm adding buttress columns at both ends of the wall for a stronger silhouette, and thinking about giving the top edge a crumbled, stepped look rather than a flat line, weighing an extruded stepped outline against using cell-based brick painting with course offsets for texture detail.

Checking that cellPaint gives enough resolution for brick-level detail by estimating texel density against paint size and surface area, it looks like plenty of texels per cell to support stone, wood, and metal materials this way, while saving textures for decorative pixel-art elements.

Then I'm reasoning through the crumbled wall silhouette—using stepped columns to vary height in brick-sized increments so the top edge reads as broken rather than smooth, adjusting column width to roughly match a brick's scale.

Working out the extrusion direction so the wall thickness sits correctly along z, centered on the drawing coordinates for proper placement.

Still writing brick pattern logic...

For the floor, I'm planning flagstones using cell painting on the top face, with irregular rectangular tiles sized by row using hashed randomization for natural variation.

I need to work out the extrusion axes for the floor outline—since it's drawn in the x/y plane but the floor itself lies flat, I'm computing the thickness direction via a cross product to get it pointing straight up, so the outline extrudes correctly into a flat slab. Then I'll work on making the floor edges ragged rather than perfectly rectangular.

I'm defining the floor's ragged outline using stepped column widths across a 2.8m by 2.2m area, with roughly 28 narrow columns whose front edges jitter randomly by a cell or two while the back edge stays flush against the wall, then setting the slab thickness and vertical offset so it sits centered properly.

With the floor top established at F=0.08, I'll treat that as the baseline height and offset all object y-coordinates by F, then start laying out the scene objects from left to right along the viewer's X axis.

Now I'm positioning the wall (thickness 0.3, centered at z=-0.8, spanning x from -1.3 to 1.3) and the floor (depth 2.2), then placing the chest centered at x=0, z=-0.25, keeping it axis-aligned rather than rotated so the pixel-art cell painting stays crisp. Next I'm figuring out torch placement along the wall.

Now I'm working out the barrel cluster on the right side of the floor—a few standing barrels of varying size near the chest, one lying on its side along the x-axis so it stays grid-aligned, plus a broken barrel with missing staves and an open barrel with its lid leaning beside it for variety.

For the left side, I'm placing the spike trap plate around (-0.5, 0.5), a bone pile further out near the far corner, and a dropped torch nearby, keeping the whole scene roughly 2.4 units wide by 2.0 deep. Now I'm detailing the spike trap itself with a recessed pit framed by a raised stone border.

Inside, I'm laying out a 4x4 grid of iron pyramid spikes at varied heights -- some fully extended, some half-raised, some retracted into empty holes -- with rust highlights and blood-stain decals at the base cells, and considering adding a skeleton reaching into the pit for extra grim detail. Since I have plenty of part budget, I'll keep each spike and hole as separate objects rather than merging them.

I'm also planning joints for the trap: a root joint plus a chestLid hinge for the lid, and making sure every non-lid part is explicitly assigned to the root bone so nothing accidentally inherits the lid's joint by proximity. I'll write a small helper function to handle part placement cleanly.

Now I'm working out the color palette, keeping to flat colors sparingly and relying mostly on cellPaint ramps for the stone textures with cool bluish dungeon-gray tones.

Still defining color ramps...

I'm also working out a cell-based wood plank texture for the chest front, dividing the surface into horizontal plank rows with seam lines and randomized darker speckles for grain variation.

For the lid, I'm considering a barrel-vaulted shape built from faceted stepped boxes or a half-octagon arch profile extruded along one axis, working through the coordinate math for how the arch cross-section should be oriented and extruded.

Computing stepped arch heights...

Now I'm thinking through the lid's iron bands, planning to reuse the arch outline function but grown by a cell margin on each side and in height, offset slightly in z so it sits above the lid surface.

Then for the chest body I'm sketching a box with inset plank panels, plus iron corner brackets and vertical bands for detail.

For the interior, I want an open chest with the lid tilted back, revealing a dark inside holding a heap of gold coins built from stacked voxel boxes with a speckled gold ramp, topped with coin disc cylinders and a few spilled coins and gems in front for extra flair.

I'm thinking of giving the gems (ruby, emerald, sapphire) a modest glow around 0.5, reserving stronger glow for the flames and embers, while keeping the body construction simple using a floor slab plus four wall boxes with a raised interior floor to hold the coin pile.

For richer detail, I want to add thin red cloth lining panels inside the walls to contrast against the wood, plus a trim at the top rim, giving the chest a nicer red-and-gold interior look. I'm now working out the hinge joint placement at the back top of the body to connect the lid.

Working through the rotation geometry: since the lid extends forward from the hinge, opening it means the front edge needs to rise, so I'm figuring out whether the pose rotation should be positive or negative around the x-axis to get that lifting motion correct.

Checking the hinge position more carefully — at that depth the open lid would clip the back wall, so I'm shifting the chest forward slightly, repositioning the hinge to around z=-0.4 so the swinging arch clears the wall boundary with margin.

Now moving on to the wall torches: I'm planning an iron bracket with a flat backplate against the wall, a ring holder to cradle the torch, a diagonal support brace, and a wooden shaft angled outward from the wall.

The torch head needs charred pitch-black top with cloth stripe wraps, and the flame itself I'll build from crossed billboard cards with layered colors -- outer red-orange, smaller inner yellow -- plus tiny glowing embers and spark particles floating above, and maybe a soft warm glow patch painted on the wall behind it.

For the wall paint I want to compute warmth based on distance from each torch position, shifting the stone color ramp toward orange tones near the light source, using a separate warm-toned ramp with dithering for a pixelated soft falloff. I'm also considering whether the floor should pick up some of that warm glow near the chest area, though the actual lighting will come from the real scene lights anyway.

Now I'm adding moss patches at the base of walls using noise thresholds combined with low y-position checks, plus thin crack lines detected where noise value sits close to 0.5. For the barrel I'm sketching a lathed profile with a bulge in the middle, defining radius-vs-height points to shape it into a rounded octagonal form.

For the metal hoops I'm building thin ring-band profiles offset slightly outward from the barrel's radius at each height, placing four hoops near the top and bottom, then giving them an iron look with rust speckle via cellPaint.

The top of the barrel is just the flat end of the lathe profile, so I'm painting it with world-aligned wood planks and a darker inset rim near the edge, using a barrel-specific paint closure that has access to the axis center coordinates. For the staves, I'm computing angular sectors around the barrel axis to place seams between planks, quantizing by angle fraction to decide where seams fall.

Since the seam thickness won't be perfectly uniform across cells, I'm accepting some approximation there, and adding per-stave color variation via hashing, plus knot speckles and a y-based lighting gradient. I also want warm torch light to influence nearby barrels, so I'm defining a warmth function based on distance to torch positions that shifts the wood color ramp brighter near the light source.

For the decals, I'm sketching small 11×11 pixel icons on the barrels instead of text -- a skull mark on one barrel to signal danger and a red cross-mark on another.

Deciding on a halved texel size of 0.01 for finer detail work, giving a size around 0.12m for small decal regions. For bones like the skull, I'm thinking of using a Minecraft-style skin sheet layout at roughly 0.0125 scale per face.

Sketching out the skull dimensions at this resolution—around 18×16×20 pixels for the cranium and a smaller jaw box—so I can plan eye sockets, nasal cavity, and teeth details onto the UV faces, placing dark eye socket regions and other features on the front face layout.

For placement I'm thinking of multiple skull instances with varied poses: one impaled on a spike, one in a bone pile, maybe a smaller one near the chest, each reusing the texture with different rotations. Then moving on to the ribcage—spine vertebrae segments plus curved rib arcs built from smaller box pieces.

Each rib is a thin curved sweep along a planar arc, using a flat bone-tone color with subtle shading or darker tips for variation. I'm planning 6 ribs per side plus a sternum and a 7-vertebra spine, posing the whole ribcage as if collapsed and lying on its back on the floor.

For positioning, the spine runs along one axis near the floor, with rib pairs arcing up from each vertebra and curving outward and down, one side lower than the other to show the collapse. I'm working out the arc math for each rib so it rises from the spine, bows outward to a radius, then curves back toward where the sternum would be.

Still tuning rib geometry...

For the ribs I'll use a boxy cross-section for that pixel-blocky look, with tapered radii for each sweep. Then I'm thinking through the femurs as rod shapes with box sections and bulb joint ends, plus whether to bother extruding a pelvis outline or skip it for simplicity.

I'm also considering adding an arm reaching toward the trap — forearm rods plus a hand with a palm box and tiny finger rods — to suggest a failed adventurer's story, though I'm wary of overcomplicating the set with extras like a sword or helmet.

Scoping the build to roughly 350-450 parts, I'm planning the clutter details — coins, webs, rubble, moss, shackles, a dropped torch — alongside the core props. For the build code, I'm working out the part and rod APIs, checking rotation conventions and section options for the rod sweeps, then moving into the pixel kit for cell painting.

Now I'm sketching out the helper module imports — builder, frame, rng, noise, pixel kit utilities, and a glow kit — while being careful about unused imports causing typecheck errors, and verifying the geometry merge utility's import path works with the project's tsconfig. I'm also considering snapping all palette colors through a quantization function to get that retro, limited-color look.

Writing torch lighting function...

Now I'm defining a paint function for stone brick walls using coursed brick rows based on vertical pixel position.

Still refining brick shading...

Writing ramp index math...

Still writing wood paint logic...

I'm now setting up gold speckle paint and thinking about the texture atlas layout, then moving into concrete floor coordinates -- mapping drawing-space x/y to world x/z with the floor starting at -1.4 and extruded to thickness F.

Working out the floor's jagged front edge versus flush back edge across its 28x22 grid of 0.1m cells, then figuring out how the flagstone paint pattern (0.02m cells) tiles across the slab's sides.

Now I'm placing scene details: rubble near the broken floor edge, a spike trap in front within the floor bounds, bones piled to one side, a chest in the middle, barrels off to the right, and torches flanking the bone pile. I'm sketching coordinates for a standing barrel near the chest.

Checking barrel placements against the chest and against each other, I notice two barrels and a lying barrel overlap slightly near the right edge, so I need to nudge one barrel's position to clear the collision while keeping everything inside the floor bounds.

For the lying barrel I'm rethinking the paint logic to support different orientations — rotating it so its axis runs along x instead of y, and adding chocks to keep it from rolling. I'll generalize the barrel-painting function to accept an axis parameter so it can compute stave angles correctly whether the barrel stands upright or lies on its side.

Still writing barrel profile points...

I'm thinking about filling the barrel interior with a dark murky green liquid disc, maybe with a small highlight pixel for texture. I also want to add a closed lid barrel with rim planks, plus a smaller broken lid leaning against it for variety.

For the lying barrel, I'll add a bung hole on the belly and a brass spigot on the end cap to make it feel functional. I'm also planning other clutter elements like coins, rubble, webs, shackles, moss, and a tiny skeleton hand clutching a coin, along with a pixel-art radial cobweb tucked into a corner between the wall and floor.

Now I'm positioning the cobweb as a transparent decal in the wall's upper-left corner near the torch, then working out wall-mounted shackles above the chest with hanging chains made of alternating link segments.

I need to check for clearance between the chest lid's open position and the hanging shackles, so I'm raising the staple to y=1.5 with a shorter chain so the manacles end well above the lid's bulge. The wall crumbles near the top around y 1.68, and I'm placing the torch brackets at y F+1.0 with flames rising just above that.

Now I'm figuring out the wall's vertical extent — it should run from near the floor (sinking slightly into the slab, since the overlap is hidden) up to about F+1.78, so I'll extrude the outline from y=0.02 to 1.78.

I'm also planning buttress columns at the wall's ends, thin pillars around x=±1.22 with some protrusion from the wall face, to give it structural depth.

I'll give these pillars a stepped capital and base plinth using slightly wider boxes, painted to match the wall. Skipping extra details like alcoves or banners, I'll instead focus on torch sconces: a small iron backplate mounted flush against the wall front with rivets and a ring-shaped holder for the torch.

For the torch itself, I'm shaping the shaft as a leaning rod held by a bracket arm connecting the wall plate to a ring around the shaft's middle. The torch head will be a tapered box wrapped in painted cloth bands, darkening to soot-black near the top where flame cards will sit.

Now I'm sketching the flame as pixel art, hand-drawing rows of a 12-wide grid to build the shape from red outer edges through orange and yellow toward a white-hot core.

For the torch head I'm setting up crossed flame cards facing upward with glow strength, plus extra ember cubes and licks for detail, and planning the chest's wood-paneled walls, bottom slab, and darker corner feet blocks.

Now I'm adding the iron hardware: vertical corner brackets slightly overlapping the body edges, horizontal straps across the front and lid, and a gold lock plate with a keyhole decal and hasp connecting lid to body.

I'm also planning the handles as iron rings with staples at the sides, twin hinge knuckles at the back, and a red interior liner, then building the coin heap as stepped gold boxes topped with scattered individual coin cylinders.

I'm adding a few jeweled octahedron gems in red, blue, and green with glow, plus a couple of gold bars, and scattering spilled coins and a small stack in front of the chest, then sizing the lid arch dimensions.

Now I'm working out the lid's curved arch profile cell by cell, computing height based on distance from center to get a dome shape, and setting up the extrusion direction for the lid geometry.

The hinge needs to sit at the back-bottom edge of the lid where it pivots against the chest body, and I need to make sure the painted texture stays fixed to the lid's local geometry rather than shifting when it rotates open.

Since parts added after posing won't inherit that pose, I should pose the lid last, once all its sub-parts are built. For the trap, I'm laying out a sunken floor with a raised stone border frame and a darker iron-ish inset plate sitting on top of the floor.

Now I'm working out the spike holes on the iron plate: a 4×4 grid spaced 0.15 apart, each a dark square hole with an iron collar, paired with a four-sided cone spike whose paint shades from rusty iron at the base to a lighter tip, with some spikes getting dripping blood/red accents near the top.

I'm defining a height pattern matrix for the sixteen spikes, with 0.0 meaning a retracted hole with just a rusty cap, and 0.30 meaning a tall spike -- one of which, at row1/col1, gets a skull impaled on its tip, tilted roughly 15 degrees with the jaw dropped open, positioned so the spike pokes up through the cranium interior.

Now I'm detailing the pressure plate borders with carved rune/skull decals, hazard-stripe or chevron paint, blood speckles, scattered pebbles and a broken arrow, plus corner rivets and bolts, and adding dried blood splatter patches to the floor paint near the trap based on distance and noise thresholds.

Then I'm placing a dropped torch near the bones -- a shaft lying on the floor with a charred head and glowing embers -- positioning it and an arm/hand relative to the trap and bones regions. I'm laying out the skeleton itself around that same area: a segmented spine with vertebrae and spinous processes, ribs in pairs along the spine, and femurs positioned near the pelvis region.

I'm defining a helper function that builds a bone as a rod with a tapered box section plus small knob boxes at each end, meant to be reused for femurs, tibias, humeri, and ulnas. Then I'm scattering skulls and loose bone fragments around the floor -- a larger skull near the wall base, a smaller one tucked in a nook, plus vertebra and finger-bone debris -- and positioning a forearm skeleton with a palm and thin finger rods reaching out toward the edge of the spike trap.

Now I'm thinking through realistic proportions: sizing the skull and cranium boxes close to actual human dimensions, widening the ribcage to around 0.28-0.3 to match real ribcage width, and settling on a slightly smaller, stylized barrel size (0.8 height, 0.29 radius) with chunky proportions, then working out the chest and pillar placement coordinates around it.

I'm now carefully checking for collisions between the barrel props and the pillar, nudging positions and sizes slightly so they don't overlap, then adjusting the chest's x-range to keep clutter tight but non-intersecting before moving on to placing prop B.

Checking C's position against the floor's front jagged edge, I realize the lying prop overhangs the floor boundary, so I'm extending the floor's depth and reducing the jag amount to keep everything contained.

Now I'm verifying clearances between the trapdoor, chest, and hinge positions, making sure the chest's open lid arc and the trapdoor bounds don't collide with the front wall, and placing spilled coins just in front of the chest within the clear floor area.

Next I'm positioning the scattered bones and ribcage away from the left pillar, checking the skull sits flush near the wall, and plotting the dropped torch's angled position along with the hand and forearm bones so they stay clear of the trapdoor's x-boundary.

Now I'm placing the two torches symmetrically on either side of the chest, verifying the barrel sits beneath one torch and the bone pile beneath the other for the dungeon atmosphere. Then I'm reconsidering the wall extrusion's vertical origin and z-thickness to make sure the floor slab and wall base don't overlap awkwardly.

Since the wall's bottom edge coincides with the floor's top, I'm deciding to add a baseboard detail where they meet, but opting for moss and rubble texture instead of extra geometry, plus scattering some moss patches for extra grime.

I'm also adding a small cluster of glowing teal mushrooms near the base of the wall for a cute dungeon accent, building each from a thin stem box and a domed lathe cap.

Overall the prop group sizing checks out fine, so now I'm moving to writing the actual code, setting up the builder and root joint structure. Setting up the builder structure...

Finishing the warm stone ramp values, then writing a small integer hash function for generating deterministic ids from coordinate pairs...

Adding torch light sources that fall off over distance, and now building the texture mapping for wall and pillar stone courses with brick-like offset rows...

Still writing brick pattern logic...

Still working out moss density...then for floors I'm setting up flag/tile patterns based on which axis is dominant, computing row indices from position coordinates.

Adding blood stain decals...

I also need a wood plank painting function, dividing each face into planks along one axis with per-plank color variation via hashed noise, keeping orientation consistent per box face.

For realism I'm adding grain streaks via periodic noise bands, occasional dark knots at low random probability, lighter highlight edges along plank boundaries, and dark seam lines between planks, then warming the color slightly based on lighting intensity.

For chest construction I'm sizing planks at 0.1m height giving 4 bands on the 0.4m body. Then I'm defining iron paint with noise-based shading, directional highlights where surface normal points up, and rust speckling using layered noise thresholds against a rust color ramp. Gold paint follows a similar pattern with random brightness variation and top-facing highlights, while bone elements get flat coloring for now.

Now I'm extending bone paint to femur rods and knobs using the same cell-based approach with vertical noise shading, keeping consistency across all bone parts, and applying light dithering to rib sweeps for subtlety. I'm noting that pixelated textures should magnify without smoothing to preserve the chunky atlas look.

Writing barrel paint function...

Adding ambient occlusion darkening near barrel ends, separating hoops with iron paint, and starting the barrel-building helper function with a lathe profile defined by radius-per-height points.

Maybe I'll go with 10 segments for a rounder barrel, trying a spin offset to align a face forward, then placing a decal on the barrel front using a position and direction near the front face.

For the barrel's interior, I want the inner wall to appear darker by checking whether the surface normal points inward toward the axis, darkening those faces accordingly. I'm sketching the lathe outline points that bulge outward from the axis and return, keeping x non-negative since it traces from the axis out and back for a closed barrel shape.

Closing the shape back to the axis without crossing, then adding the murky liquid contents: a flat slime-colored disc near the floor and maybe a small floating object inside.

I'll keep barrel B's contents as dark stagnant water with a subtle highlight rather than glowing green, letting mushrooms carry the teal glow instead and torches carry the one strong warm accent. Now I'm writing the loop that places wall torches symmetrically on both sides...

Still writing torch geometry...

Shaft endpoint sits at F+1.22, and I'm defining a helper to compute shaft position at any y, tapering the head box from narrow near the shaft to wider at the top.

For texture, I'm giving the wrapping cloth alternating stripe bands and charring the top with black and glowing orange ember speckles, plus a thin rod cross-section for the shaft.

For the flame, I'm attaching a billboard card facing upward at the torch tip, sized to roughly match the flame texture's pixel dimensions, then applying a glow effect to the resulting mesh.

I'm adding a smaller inner flame layer for brightness, a handful of tiny floating ember cube sprites merged into a single glowing mesh, and a wall-mounted dropped torch variant with its own tilted shaft, charred frustum head, and ember glow, while skipping smoke effects for simplicity.

For rubble, I'm scattering randomly-rotated boxes around the wall base, merging them by color into grayscale groups for flat-shaded stones. For the bone piles, I'm combining skull pieces, rib sweeps, and vertebrae into merged parts painted with a shared bone cell texture, keeping everything as single consolidated meshes for efficiency.

Now I'm designing the texture layout for the skull, carving out eye sockets and jaw detail pixel by pixel on the cranium and jaw UV faces.

Still designing the jaw box and teeth placement...

Computing sheet width from skull layout dimensions, then writing a per-face fill function that blends bone-colored noise with vertical shading for each box face...

Now I'm assigning darkness levels per face direction (top lightest, bottom darkest) with dithered noise blended in, and deciding whether skull eye sockets should get a subtle red glow or stay plainly dark.

For the chest lock, I'm planning to texture a small box's front face with a gold plate design including a keyhole, bevel, and screws, accepting that the same texture wraps all six faces negligibly.

For gems, I'll use faceted octahedron shapes colored ruby, sapphire, and emerald with flat shading and a subtle glow. Then I'm thinking through the lid: arched extrusion with iron bands, a front hasp box, and hinge knuckles connecting it to the body.

Adding hinge cylinders...

I also want chest feet, cloth lining, and worn wood texture with chipped corner specks for aging, plus a pile of gold coin boxes filling the interior floor.

I'm now blocking out the chest body itself: a bottom slab, front/back/side wall panels sized and positioned around the feet height, then a thin interior liner region to simulate fabric padding inside.

Rather than filling the interior with a solid block, I'll add thin quilted-cloth liner panels just inside each wall face, painted with a diamond stitch pattern using a modulo trick on texture coordinates, plus a trim ring near the top rim.

For the coin pile, I'm stacking four tapered heap layers that get narrower and taller toward the center, jittering their positions slightly for a natural look, then painting them gold with speckled noise to mimic scattered coins, topped with individual coin discs and a subtle gold glow.

Now I'm working out a procedural cobweb texture, drawing radial lines from a corner at angles stepped every 22.5 degrees plus concentric arc segments at a few radii to form a quarter-web pattern pixel by pixel.

I'll size the web plane at 0.4×0.4 with radial lines trailing down-right, positioned just off the wall front surface with a tiny z-offset to avoid clipping, and skip adding other small decor like a skull candle for now.

Now I'm setting up the TypeScript build with proper imports for THREE, geometry merging utilities, and the builder/frame helpers, making sure the part options and color types line up correctly before writing the actual scene code.

Writing scene setup code...

Figuring out the right type for the bone parameter is tricky since b.part's parameter types involve overloads, so I'm considering just typing it directly as the type of the root joint instead.

I'll define a helper that places geometry with position and rotation, then build a transform helper that composes a matrix from position and Euler rotation to apply to merged geometries.

I need to track which primitives are indexed versus non-indexed (polyhedron gems aren't indexed) so I don't merge incompatible geometries, keeping gems as separate parts. Now I'm setting up the body constants like floor height, texel size, and chest position offsets before writing the section-by-section geometry code.

Working out the lid geometry next — computing a column-height array for a rounded profile, building a stepped outline from it, and figuring out hinge position and overlap so the lid sits flush against the body walls. Building lid bands...

Still writing extrusion code...

Still defining trap border pieces...

Still placing spike holes and collars...

Adding small iron rivets at the plate corners, then placing a skull on the center spike with a tilted cranium and a fallen jaw resting nearby on the plate. I'm also scattering some broken debris and sketching a rune decal near the front border.

For the border itself, I'm bumping its height up to fit a decal properly, then abandoning the rune idea in favor of painting hazard chevron stripes across the top using alternating dark and amber cells based on a diagonal pattern.

Actually, I'll swap amber hazard stripes for a worn red-ochre chevron look instead, which fits a dungeon aesthetic better. Now I'm sketching out the mushroom clusters—a stem box with a lathed cap using a small profile curve—placed near the pillar base with moss, skipping glow decor for simplicity.

Writing wall texture code...

Still writing shading logic...

I'm working out moss placement using noise and height thresholds with dithered color picks, then applying similar logic to pillars, walls, and floor paint before moving to actual implementation. Now I'm sketching out the barrel generator function with options for openness and orientation.

For positioning, I'm figuring out standing versus lying barrels: standing ones use a lathe shape at floor height, while lying ones get rotated onto their side with a radius chosen so the octagonal cross-section sinks slightly into the floor to hide any gaps.

I'm deciding to skip chocks and instead place stones for support, and setting up shared hoop geometry that reuses the same lathe approach with an axis parameter for both orientations. Now I'm working out the paint/texture placement, parameterizing the barrel origin and orientation so the same function handles both standing and lying cases.

Writing lid cap logic...

Still writing stave shading logic...

Now I'm adding details like barrel decals, murky water inside barrel B, and a brass spigot on barrel C positioned at the belly front with a handle, plus a dark puddle on the floor beneath it to suggest dripping.

For rubble, I'm scattering small stone pebbles near the wall base and trap, varying their size and rotation and assigning them a grey color ramp, while writing a simple collision-check function that rejects placements overlapping the chest, barrels, trap, and bones so the debris stays clear of other objects.

I'm also checking texel density across the painted surfaces to make sure my floor and wall textures stay sharp enough at the chosen cell resolution before moving on to writing the actual generation code.

Now I'm building a hanging chain from a loop of small torus links positioned and rotated to hang vertically along the wall, plus a wall staple and a larger ring anchoring it, finishing with a manacle cuff at the end.

I'm also planning a second chain pair mirrored on either side with slightly different lengths for variety, and working out the open lid's geometry when rotated 95° so it occupies the back volume without clipping.

I'm weighing where to position the liner box relative to the lid base so it doesn't visually clash with the interior heap when the lid is closed, but since the closed state is only hypothetical here, the overlap isn't really a visible concern.

Writing ribs code...

Building the rib curve with catmull-rom interpolation and slight z-drift for realism, then sweeping a box-section radius function along it, with the collapsed side getting flatter and wider dimensions plus a lean. Sternum isn't needed since it's not visible, so I'm moving on to the spine's vertebrae boxes.

Now I'm placing eight vertebrae along the spine with small transverse processes, merged into one geometry, then defining a longBone helper that uses rods with box sections and knob-shaped end caps for the femurs, all grouped into a boneBits list.

For the hand, I'm building a palm box with five thin finger rods fanned out by rotation, a separate thumb, plus a wrist, and scattering ten tiny bone fragments nearby on the floor. I'm also placing the skull near the wall and a second skull caught in the trap before moving on to designing the flame ASCII art grid, laying out a 12-wide by 20-tall character map row by row.

Still designing the flame layout...

Still designing pixel patterns...

Still sketching the skull pixel grid...
